text: Polar and cylindrical coordinates: tensors and viscosity The formulas below use physical components in the orthonormal basis (e_r,e_phi,e_z), with cylindrical coordinates (r,phi,z), phi in radians, and r > 0. A planar polar field is obtained by setting u_z = 0 and all z derivatives to zero. Coordinate-basis tensor components have different metric factors; mixing the conventions creates incorrect viscous forces. THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data For a reference derivation of cylindrical fluid equations, see Richard Fitzpatrick’s lecture notes. This chapter states a general bulk-viscosity convention explicitly and checks it with analytic fields. Velocity gradient: differentiate the basis too# Let L_ij = e_i · ((e_j · grad)u). Its rows are velocity components and columns are differentiation directions: L=(∂rur(∂ϕur−uϕ)/r∂zur∂ruϕ(∂ϕuϕ+ur)/r∂zuϕ∂ruz(∂ϕuz)/r∂zuz).L=​∂r​ur​∂r​uϕ​∂r​uz​​(∂ϕ​ur​−uϕ​)/r(∂ϕ​uϕ​+ur​)/r(∂ϕ​uz​)/r​∂z​ur​∂z​uϕ​∂z​uz​​​. The terms −u_phi/r and +u_r/r arise from rotation of the basis. Define D = (L+L^T)/2 and theta = tr(L): θ=∇⋅u=∂rur+urr+∂ϕuϕr+∂zuz.θ=∇⋅u=∂r​ur​+rur​​+r∂ϕ​uϕ​​+∂z​uz​. The input partials[...,i,j] in numart.coordinates means the plain coordinate derivative of physical velocity component i with respect to coordinate j = (r,phi,z). Supply the phi derivative itself, not a derivative already divided by r. Newtonian stress: all six independent components# With total stress sigma = −p I + tau, dynamic shear viscosity mu, and bulk viscosity zeta, the three-dimensional constitutive law is τ=2μD+λθI,λ=ζ−23μ.τ=2μD+λθI,λ=ζ−32​μ. Stokes’ hypothesis sets zeta = 0. It is a material assumption, distinct from imposing incompressibility theta = 0. Positive mu and nonnegative zeta ensure nonnegative viscous dissipation. τrr=2μ ∂rur+λθ,τϕϕ=2μr(ur+∂ϕuϕ)+λθ,τzz=2μ ∂zuz+λθ,τrϕ=μ(∂ruϕ−uϕr+∂ϕurr),τrz=μ(∂zur+∂ruz),τϕz=μ(∂zuϕ+∂ϕuzr).τrr​τϕϕ​τzz​τrϕ​τrz​τϕz​​=2μ∂r​ur​+λθ,=r2μ​(ur​+∂ϕ​uϕ​)+λθ,=2μ∂z​uz​+λθ,=μ(∂r​uϕ​−ruϕ​​+r∂ϕ​ur​​),=μ(∂z​ur​+∂r​uz​),=μ(∂z​uϕ​+r∂ϕ​uz​​).​ The lower indices here label physical components, not covariant coordinate-basis components. Off-diagonal engineering shear rates are twice the corresponding D component; applying another factor of two to the formulas above would be an error. Stress divergence: the viscous force per volume# For a symmetric physical stress tensor, f = div(tau) has components fr=∂rτrr+1r∂ϕτrϕ+∂zτrz+τrr−τϕϕr,fϕ=∂rτrϕ+1r∂ϕτϕϕ+∂zτϕz+2τrϕr,fz=∂rτrz+1r∂ϕτϕz+∂zτzz+τrzr.fr​fϕ​fz​​=∂r​τrr​+r1​∂ϕ​τrϕ​+∂z​τrz​+rτrr​−τϕϕ​​,=∂r​τrϕ​+r1​∂ϕ​τϕϕ​+∂z​τϕz​+r2τrϕ​​,=∂r​τrz​+r1​∂ϕ​τϕz​+∂z​τzz​+rτrz​​.​ The acceleration contribution is f/rho. Pressure contributes −grad(p) separately. These divergence formulas allow spatially variable mu and zeta when stress derivatives include their variation. In the Python routine, partials[...,i,j,k] is the coordinate derivative k of physical stress component (i,j). Constant viscosity and the vector Laplacian# Only for constant mu and lambda can the force be simplified to f=μ∇2u+(μ+λ)∇θ.f=μ∇2u+(μ+λ)∇θ. For a scalar g, let Δsg=1r∂r(r∂rg)+1r2∂ϕ2g+∂z2g.Δs​g=r1​∂r​(r∂r​g)+r21​∂ϕ2​g+∂z2​g. The physical components of the vector Laplacian are (∇2u)r=Δsur−urr2−2r2∂ϕuϕ,(∇2u)ϕ=Δsuϕ−uϕr2+2r2∂ϕur,(∇2u)z=Δsuz.(∇2u)r​(∇2u)ϕ​(∇2u)z​​=Δs​ur​−r2ur​​−r22​∂ϕ​uϕ​,=Δs​uϕ​−r2uϕ​​+r22​∂ϕ​ur​,=Δs​uz​.​ For incompressible constant-viscosity flow, theta vanishes, but the radial and azimuthal vector-Laplacian metric terms remain. For variable coefficients, pulling mu outside derivatives omits terms 2D·grad(mu) and theta grad(lambda). Evaluate the full stress divergence instead. Axisymmetry, polar slices, and material acceleration# Axisymmetry removes phi derivatives, not the terms u_r/r, −u_phi/r, or the stress-divergence metric terms. Axisymmetric flow may still have swirl. For a planar polar slice of a three-dimensional Newtonian fluid, retain the 2mu/3 bulk correction and tau_zz = lambda theta. A genuinely two-dimensional constitutive model uses a different deviatoric trace subtraction and must be declared separately. The scalar advective derivative is D_s/Dt = partial_t + u_r partial_r + (u_phi/r) partial_phi + u_z partial_z. Vector material acceleration has extra radial and azimuthal terms: ar=DsurDt−uϕ2r,aϕ=DsuϕDt+uruϕr,az=DsuzDt.ar​=DtDs​ur​​−ruϕ2​​,aϕ​=DtDs​uϕ​​+rur​uϕ​​,az​=DtDs​uz​​. These inertial terms are different from viscous metric terms. Coordinate-basis tensors and transformations# The cylindrical coordinate basis is (partial_r,partial_phi,partial_z) = (e_r,r e_phi,e_z), with metric diag(1,r²,1). Thus physical u_phi = r u^phi, and physical tau_phi,phi = r² tau^{phi,phi} = tau_{phi,phi}^{coordinate}/r². Covariant, contravariant, and physical arrays cannot be substituted for one another without these factors. Nonzero Christoffel symbols include Gamma^r_phi,phi = −r and Gamma^phi_r,phi = Gamma^phi_phi,r = 1/r. Covariant differentiation accounts for the same basis changes included explicitly above. The Cartesian transformation uses the orthogonal matrix Q with columns e_r, e_phi, e_z: L_cart = Q L_cyl Q^T and tau_cart = Q tau_cyl Q^T. Analytic checks and the axis# Rigid rotation: u_phi = Omega r gives antisymmetric L, D = 0, and zero viscous stress. Using partial_r u_phi alone would incorrectly create shear. Pipe Poiseuille flow: u_z = Umax(1−r²/R²) gives tau_rz = −2 mu Umax r/R² and f_z = −4 mu Umax/R². Steady axial momentum requires dp/dz = f_z. Circular Couette flow: u_phi = A r+B/r gives tau_rphi = −2 mu B/r² and zero azimuthal viscous-force divergence away from boundaries. Cartesian affine fields: random constant Cartesian velocity gradients are transformed into cylindrical data and back. Constant Cartesian stresses have zero divergence after angular basis derivatives are included. The tests also verify the dissipation identity τ:D=2μDdev:Ddev+ζθ2≥0.τ:D=2μDdev​:Ddev​+ζθ2≥0. These routines require r > 0. At the axis, use regularity and analytic limits rather than replacing r by a small arbitrary number. For a smooth axisymmetric field, u_r and u_phi are O(r), and u_z = u_z(0)+O(r²). Then the axial scalar radial Laplacian tends to 2 partial_r² u_z. Nonaxisymmetric regular Cartesian fields have different component limits; even uniform Cartesian translation need not have u_r = O(r). import numpy as np from numart.coordinates import cylindrical_velocity_gradient, newtonian_stress r, omega = 0.7, 2.0 u = np.array([0., omega*r, 0.]) du = np.zeros((3,3)); du[1,0] = omega L = cylindrical_velocity_gradient(r, u, du) assert np.allclose(newtonian_stress(L), 0.) The code checks tensor identities at supplied points. A cylindrical Navier–Stokes PDE solver, axis boundary scheme, and spherical-coordinate implementation remain future work.
